job.style: a passage that starts from a common wrong idea and corrects it

passage: Many students believe that saving money is only useful if you have a large amount to put away, or that savings are simply whatever coins happen to be left in your pocket after spending on everything you desire. This is a common mistake. In reality, financial planning starts with the habit of 'saving first'—setting aside a small portion of your income immediately, even if it is just ten rupees. When you deposit this money in a bank, it does not just sit there; it grows over time because the bank pays you interest, which is a reward for keeping your money with them. Furthermore, a budget is not a rigid, unchangeable document; it is a flexible tool that helps you balance your needs, like school books, against your wants, like a new video game. You must prioritize needs to ensure your future security, including preparing for unexpected emergencies. Even if you do not earn a formal salary, any money you receive is income, and managing it wisely is a vital life skill. By tracking every small expense, you gain control over your financial future. Remember, a budget is meant to be adjusted as your situation changes, and even small, consistent savings grow significantly through interest, helping you build a safety net for life's surprises.

items.evidence: In reality, financial planning starts with the habit of 'saving first'—setting aside a small portion of your income immediately, even if it is just ten rupees.
items.q: Meena gets 100 rupees pocket money each week. What does the 'saving first' habit ask her to do?
options: Put a small part away before spending
Save whatever coins are left after spending
Wait until she can save a large amount
Buy her wants first, then save the rest
items.explain: Saving first means setting aside a small part of income right away, even just ten rupees.

wrong.why: thinks savings are leftovers after spending
thinks wants should be bought first

items.evidence: When you deposit this money in a bank, it does not just sit there; it grows over time because the bank pays you interest, which is a reward for keeping your money with them.
items.q: Asha puts 50 rupees in a bank account. Why will her money grow over time?
options: The bank pays her for leaving money with it
The bank adds a fixed gift, whatever the time
The bank locks her notes in a named box
The bank grows only big amounts of money
items.explain: The bank pays interest as a reward for keeping money with it, so savings grow.

wrong.why: thinks interest is a free gift not linked to time
thinks the bank stores her own notes
thinks only large savings are worth anything

items.evidence: Furthermore, a budget is not a rigid, unchangeable document; it is a flexible tool that helps you balance your needs, like school books, against your wants, like a new video game.
items.q: Kabir made his budget in June. In July his bus fare goes up. What should he do?
options: Change his budget to fit the new fare
Keep the June budget exactly as it was
Cut out every want for the whole year
Ignore the rise, as it is only small
items.explain: A budget is a flexible tool, not unchangeable, so Kabir should adjust it.

wrong.why: thinks a budget must never change
thinks wants are bad and must be dropped
thinks small costs are not real expenses

items.evidence: You must prioritize needs to ensure your future security, including preparing for unexpected emergencies.
items.q: Sana is saving for a new bike. Suddenly her school bag tears. What should she do with her savings?
options: Spend it on the bag, since needs come first
Keep it, since savings are only for the bike
Buy the bike first, since wants bring joy
Choose the bike, since costlier things are needs
items.explain: Needs come first, and savings also prepare us for unexpected emergencies like a torn bag.

wrong.why: thinks savings are never for emergencies
thinks wants come first because they bring happiness

items.evidence: Even if you do not earn a formal salary, any money you receive is income, and managing it wisely is a vital life skill.
items.q: Tara has no job but gets 200 rupees as a birthday gift. How should she think of it?
options: As income she should plan and manage
As a gift, since only a salary is income
As spare cash to spend as she likes
As too small an amount to bother saving
items.explain: Any money you receive is income, even without a salary, and should be managed wisely.

wrong.why: thinks income means only a salary
thinks money is for spending freely, saving leftovers
thinks small amounts are not worth saving
